questions.title: Fact-finding methods
questions.text: Match each fact-finding method to its description.

right.text: Written questions answered by many people, often anonymously
A conversation in which the analyst can ask follow-up questions
The analyst watches users doing their work
The analyst studies the forms, reports and records of the current system

scheme.mark_scheme: Questionnaire → written questions answered by many people; Interview → conversation with follow-up questions; Observation → watching users at work; Examining documents → studying forms, reports and records (1 each)
scheme.explanation: These are the four fact-finding methods named in the specification.

questions.title: Spot the closed question
questions.text: Which of the following is a **closed** question?

scheme.explanation: A closed question has a fixed set of possible answers, so the answers can be counted (quantitative data).

options.content: What do you think about the library?
How could the booking process be improved?
How many times a week do you use the library? 0 / 1–2 / 3–5 / more than 5
Why do you return books late?

questions.title: Closed questions and data
questions.text: Answers to closed questions produce **qualitative** data.

scheme.mark_scheme: False (1)
scheme.explanation: Closed questions have fixed answers that can be counted, so they produce quantitative data. Open questions produce qualitative data.

questions.title: Advantages of questionnaires
questions.text: State **two** advantages of using a questionnaire to collect information.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): reaches many people; cheap; quick to collect; can be anonymous so answers may be more honest; closed answers are quick to analyse / easy to turn into statistics; people answer in their own time; online forms total the answers automatically
scheme.model_answer: 1 It can be given to many people at low cost. 2 It can be anonymous, so people may answer honestly.

questions.title: Disadvantages of questionnaires and interviews
questions.text: State **two** disadvantages of using questionnaires and **two** disadvantages of using interviews when collecting data.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Questionnaire (any two): low response rate; questions cannot be explained / may be misunderstood; limited depth / no follow-up questions; careless or untrue answers

Interview (any two): time-consuming; only a few people can be interviewed; expensive; not anonymous so answers may not be honest; depends on the interviewer's skill; answers are harder to analyse
scheme.model_answer: Questionnaire: low response rate; questions cannot be explained. Interview: time-consuming so only a few people are interviewed; not anonymous so people may not be honest.
scheme.ai_instructions: Each answer must apply to that method. Do not credit the same point twice in one method.

questions.title: A disadvantage of observation
questions.text: Explain **one** disadvantage of using **observation** to collect information about a system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Disadvantage (1) + explanation (1): people may behave differently when watched (1) so the analyst may not see how the system is normally used (1); time-consuming (1) because the analyst must watch for a long time / several days (1); rare events / problems may not be seen (1) so some problems are missed (1); does not show opinions (1) so reasons for problems are unknown (1)
scheme.model_answer: Staff may work faster or more carefully when they know they are being watched, so the analyst does not see how the system is really used.

questions.title: An advantage of examining documents
questions.text: State **one** advantage of analysing the existing documentation of a system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): shows the exact data items / formats used; quick / cheap; does not disturb staff; shows the volume of data; gives facts for the data dictionary / screen design
scheme.model_answer: It shows exactly which data items are recorded on the current forms.

questions.title: Choosing a fact-finding method
questions.text: Tick **one** box in each row to show the most suitable fact-finding method for each situation.

prefill: Finding the opinions of 500 students about the canteen
Finding out the director's detailed needs for monthly reports
Measuring how long a cashier takes to serve one customer
Finding which data items appear on the current order forms

scheme.mark_scheme: Opinions of 500 students → questionnaire; director's needs → interview; serving time → observation; data items on forms → examining documents (1 per row)
scheme.explanation: Many people → questionnaire; one key person needing detail → interview; real times → observation; exact data items → documents.

questions.title: Types of interview
questions.text: Match each type of interview to its description.

right.text: The same prepared questions are asked in the same order to everyone
Prepared questions, plus follow-up questions depending on the answers
An open conversation about the topic without fixed questions

scheme.mark_scheme: Structured → same questions in the same order; Semi-structured → prepared questions plus follow-ups; Unstructured → open conversation (1 each)
scheme.explanation: Semi-structured interviews are the most common: they combine comparable answers with follow-up questions.

questions.title: Spot the leading question
questions.text: Which question should **not** be used in a questionnaire because it is a **leading** question?

scheme.explanation: A leading question pushes the person towards a particular answer, so the results are biased.

options.content: How often do you use the school website?
Don't you agree that the old paper system is far too slow?
Which device do you usually use: phone, tablet or computer?
On a scale of 1–5, how easy is it to book a room?

questions.title: Quantitative or qualitative?
questions.text: Tick **one** box in each row to show whether the data is **quantitative** or **qualitative**.

prefill: The number of books borrowed each day
Librarians' opinions about the current system
The average time students wait to borrow a book
The reasons students give for returning books late
Students' ratings of the library from 1 to 5

scheme.mark_scheme: Number of books → quantitative; opinions → qualitative; average time → quantitative; reasons → qualitative; ratings 1–5 → quantitative (1 each)
scheme.explanation: Numbers, times, counts and ratings are quantitative; opinions and reasons in words are qualitative.

questions.title: Calculating a percentage
questions.text: In a survey, **54** of **120** students said they had lost a library card. Calculate the percentage of students who had lost a card.

questions.title: Mean rating
questions.text:
Eight users rated the current booking system from 1 (very poor) to 5 (very good):

`4, 5, 3, 4, 2, 4, 5, 3`

Calculate the **mean** rating.

scheme.explanation: Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values.

questions.title: Analysing data
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

Qualitative answers are analysed by grouping similar comments into [[1]]. Quantitative results are often shown in a bar or pie [[2]]. Checking a result by using two different fact-finding methods is called [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) themes (2) chart (3) triangulation
scheme.explanation: Thematic analysis groups comments into themes; charts present numbers; triangulation compares results from different methods.

questions.title: Qualitative analysis
questions.text: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of **qualitative** data analysis.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): detailed / rich information; explains reasons and feelings; can reveal unexpected problems

Disadvantage (1): subjective / open to interpretation; slow / hard to analyse; usually a small sample; hard to compare or show in charts
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: it explains why users have problems. Disadvantage: it is slow to analyse and can be subjective.

questions.title: Compare quantitative and qualitative analysis
questions.text: Compare **quantitative** and **qualitative** methods of data analysis.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 comparison points, each referring to both (1 each):
- quantitative uses numbers / qualitative uses words, opinions
- quantitative analysed with statistics, percentages, charts / qualitative by grouping into themes
- quantitative is objective and quick to analyse / qualitative is subjective and slow
- quantitative shows how many / how big a problem is / qualitative explains why
- quantitative works with large samples / qualitative usually small samples
scheme.model_answer: Quantitative analysis works with numbers such as counts and ratings, while qualitative analysis works with words such as opinions. Quantitative data is analysed with percentages and charts, qualitative data by grouping comments into themes. Quantitative analysis is quicker and more objective, but qualitative analysis gives more detail and explains why users have problems. Quantitative analysis can use large samples; qualitative analysis usually uses a few people.
scheme.ai_instructions: A point only counts if it compares both methods (explicitly or with 'whereas'). Max 4.

questions.title: From a finding to a requirement
questions.text:
By **observing** the librarians, an analyst found that issuing one book on paper cards takes about **3 minutes**, causing long queues.

Write **one** requirement for the new system based on this finding.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A requirement about issuing books faster, e.g. using barcode scanning / automatic recording (1)
- that is specific / measurable, e.g. in under 10–30 seconds (1)

points.criterion: Requirement that solves the slow issuing problem

scheme.model_answer: The system must issue a book by scanning the book's and the student's barcodes in under 10 seconds.

questions.title: Using collected data
questions.text:
Complete the steps for using collected data to develop a new system.

1. Collect the data using fact-finding [[1]].
2. Analyse the data and identify the [[2]] of the current system.
3. Compare the alternative [[3]].
4. Write the [[4]] specification for the new system.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) methods (2) problems (3) solutions (4) requirements
scheme.explanation: Fact-finding → analysis of problems and needs → compare solutions → requirements specification.

questions.title: Weighted scoring
questions.text:
An analyst compares solutions using weighted scoring. The weights are: **Cost 3**, **Fit to requirements 5**, **Time to introduce 2**. Solution A scores **4** for cost, **3** for fit and **5** for time.

Calculate the weighted total for Solution A.

scheme.mark_scheme: 4 × 3 = 12, 3 × 5 = 15, 5 × 2 = 10 (1 for at least two correct products) (1 for all three) → total 37 (1)
scheme.explanation: Multiply each score by the weight of its criterion and add the results.

questions.title: Criteria for comparing solutions
questions.text: State **three** criteria that an analyst could use to compare alternative solutions to a problem.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): how well it meets the requirements; cost (purchase, development, training, running); time to introduce; hardware needed / compatibility; ease of use / training needed; support and updates; security; reliability; scalability / future growth; legal issues
scheme.model_answer: 1 Cost. 2 How well it meets the requirements. 3 Time needed to introduce it.
scheme.ai_instructions: The three criteria must be different.

questions.title: Off-the-shelf or bespoke?
questions.text:
A small dental clinic needs a system to book appointments. It has a **small budget** and wants to start using the system **within a month**. Its needs are similar to those of other clinics.

Compare **off-the-shelf** software with **bespoke** software for the clinic and recommend one.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Comparison (max 3, each referring to both):
- off-the-shelf is cheaper / bespoke is expensive (1)
- off-the-shelf is available immediately / bespoke takes a long time to develop (1)
- bespoke matches the requirements exactly / off-the-shelf may lack features or include unneeded ones (1)
- off-the-shelf is widely tested with support / bespoke support only from the developer (1)

Recommendation (1): off-the-shelf, justified by the small budget, one-month deadline and common needs

points.criterion: Recommends off-the-shelf with a justification from the scenario

scheme.model_answer: Off-the-shelf booking software is cheaper and can be installed at once, whereas bespoke software is expensive and takes months to write. Bespoke software would match the clinic's needs exactly, but the clinic's needs are similar to other clinics, so off-the-shelf software will cover them. Off-the-shelf is recommended because of the small budget and the one-month deadline.
scheme.ai_instructions: Comparison points must refer to both options. The recommendation mark needs a reason from the scenario.

questions.title: Comparing algorithms as solutions
questions.text:
A school system must find a student's record among **5000 records sorted by student ID** many times a day.

Explain why a **binary search** is a more effective solution than a **linear search**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Binary search halves the number of records to check after each comparison (1)
- so at most about 13 comparisons are needed instead of up to 5000 with linear search / O(log n) vs O(n) (1)

points.criterion: Binary search halves the search area each step
Comparison: about 13 vs up to 5000 comparisons / log n vs n

scheme.model_answer: Each comparison in a binary search discards half of the remaining records, so 5000 records need at most 13 comparisons, while a linear search may need to check all 5000.
scheme.explanation: 2¹³ = 8192 ≥ 5000, so the worst case is 13 comparisons.

questions.title: Functional or non-functional?
questions.text: Tick **one** box in each row to show whether each requirement is **functional** or **non-functional**.

prefill: Teachers can add and delete student records
Search results appear in under 2 seconds
The system emails a reminder two days before a book is due
Only staff who log in with a password can edit marks

scheme.mark_scheme: Add/delete records → functional; under 2 seconds → non-functional (performance); reminder emails → functional; password to edit → non-functional (security) (1 each)
scheme.explanation: Functional requirements say what the system does; non-functional requirements say how well it must work (speed, security, usability).

questions.title: Making a requirement testable
questions.text:
An analyst wrote the requirement: *"The app should be fast."*

Rewrite it as a **specific, testable** requirement and explain why your version is better.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Rewritten with a measurable value, e.g. 'The timetable page must load in under 3 seconds' (1)
- Better because it can be measured / tested at the evaluation stage (1)

points.criterion: Explains that it can be tested / measured

scheme.model_answer: "The timetable must open in under 3 seconds on a school tablet." It can be measured and tested when the system is evaluated, unlike 'fast'.

questions.title: Requirements from a scenario
questions.text:
A sports club takes court bookings by telephone and writes them in a notebook. Bookings are often written twice for the same time, and members cannot see which courts are free. The manager wants members to book online and to receive a confirmation.

State **three** system requirements for the new booking system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three requirements linked to the scenario (1 each): members must be able to book a court online; the system must show which courts / times are free; the system must prevent double bookings of the same court and time; the system must send a confirmation (email/SMS) after booking; members must log in / be identified; the manager must be able to view / cancel bookings
scheme.model_answer: 1 The system must let members book a court online. 2 The system must show which courts are free at each time and prevent double bookings. 3 The system must send a confirmation email after each booking.
scheme.ai_instructions: Requirements must come from the scenario and be different. Do not credit vague requirements such as 'easy to use'.

questions.title: A new system for a fitness club
questions.text: A fitness club with **800 members** takes class bookings by telephone. The receptionist writes the bookings on paper. Members complain that the phone is often busy, and some classes are overbooked. The manager asks an analyst to investigate before a new system is developed.

parts.title: Choosing a method
parts.text: Suggest **one** fact-finding method for collecting the opinions of all 800 members. Justify your choice.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Questionnaire / online survey (1)
- because it can reach many / all 800 members quickly and cheaply / can be anonymous (1)

points.criterion: Justification: many members, cheap, quick, anonymous

scheme.model_answer: An online questionnaire, because it can reach all 800 members quickly and cheaply.

parts.title: Percentage
parts.text: **280** of the 800 members said they had been unable to get through on the phone. Calculate this as a percentage.

parts.title: Why qualitative data too
parts.text: Explain why the analyst should also collect **qualitative** data, for example by interviewing the receptionist.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Qualitative data explains the reasons / gives detail about problems (1)
- e.g. why classes are overbooked / how the receptionist records bookings, which numbers alone do not show (1)

points.criterion: Linked to the scenario (e.g. why overbooking happens)

scheme.model_answer: The survey shows how many members have problems, but an interview explains why — for example, how the receptionist records bookings and why classes become overbooked.

parts.title: Requirements
parts.text: State **three** requirements for the new booking system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three linked to the scenario (1 each): members must book classes online / in an app; the system must show the number of free places; the system must stop bookings when a class is full; the system must send a confirmation; the receptionist must be able to view / change bookings; members must log in
scheme.model_answer: 1 Members must be able to book classes online. 2 The system must stop accepting bookings when a class is full. 3 The system must send each member a booking confirmation.
scheme.ai_instructions: Requirements must be different and come from the scenario.

summary: Methods of collecting information about a system, qualitative and quantitative analysis, comparing alternative solutions and writing system requirements.

blocks.content: Before a new system can be designed, the **systems analyst** must understand how the **current system** works, what is wrong with it and what the people who will use the new system need. This is called **fact-finding** and happens in the **analysis** stage of the SDLC.

items.title: What the analyst wants to find out
items.content:
- The **inputs, processes, outputs and storage** of the current system.
- The **problems**: slow processes, errors, lost data, queues, duplicated work.
- The **needs** of each group of users.
- The **volume** of data (how many orders, customers, records per day).
- **Constraints**: budget, deadline, hardware, laws.

items.title: Who the analyst asks (stakeholders)
items.content:
- The **client** / manager who pays for the system.
- The **end users** who will work with it every day.
- **Customers** affected by it (students, patients, shoppers).
- **Technical staff** who will maintain it.

blocks.content:
flowchart LR
  F[Fact-finding: questionnaires, interviews, observation, documents] --> A[Analyse the data: quantitative and qualitative]
  A --> P[Identify problems and needs]
  P --> O[Compare alternative solutions]
  O --> R[Requirements specification]
blocks.caption: From fact-finding to a requirements specification

blocks.content: The four fact-finding methods named in the specification are **questionnaires**, **interviews**, **observation** and **examining (analysing) existing documents**. Learn at least two advantages and two disadvantages of each.
A set of written questions given to **many people** — on paper or online (e.g. Google Forms). Answers are collected and analysed later.

blocks.title: Types of question
rows: "Have you ever lost a library book? Yes / No"
"How do you pay for lunch? Cash / Card / Kaspi QR"
"The queue is too long: 1 strongly disagree … 5 strongly agree"
"What would you change about the canteen?"
Qualitative data, detailed but harder to analyse

blocks.title: Designing a good questionnaire
items: Decide exactly **what you need to find out**.
Use **short, clear** questions — one idea per question; avoid technical words.
Avoid **leading** questions ("Don't you agree the old system is terrible?").
Use mostly **closed** questions (easy to analyse) and a few **open** ones for detail.
Keep it **short** so people finish it; explain its purpose and keep it **anonymous** if possible.
**Test** it on a few people first (pilot) and correct unclear questions.

blocks.title: Questionnaires
rows: Often a **low response rate** — many people do not reply
Can be **anonymous**, so people may answer **honestly**
Questions **cannot be explained** — they may be misunderstood
Closed answers are **quick to analyse** (counts, percentages, charts)
**Limited depth** — no follow-up questions; complex views are hard to capture
People may give careless or untrue answers
Online forms collect and total the answers automatically

blocks.content: A **face-to-face (or online) conversation** in which the analyst asks one person or a small group questions about the system.

items.title: Structured
items.content: The same prepared questions in the same order for everyone — easy to compare answers.

items.title: Semi-structured
items.content: Prepared questions plus **follow-up** questions depending on the answers — the most common type.

items.title: Unstructured
items.content: An open conversation about the topic — very detailed but hard to compare and analyse.

blocks.title: Interviews
rows: **Detailed** answers; the analyst can ask **follow-up** questions
**Time-consuming** — only a **few people** can be interviewed
Questions can be **explained** if they are not understood
**Expensive** — the analyst's and the interviewee's time
The analyst can see **reactions** and body language
Not anonymous, so people may **not be honest** or may say what the boss wants to hear
Answers depend on the interviewer's skill; notes are hard to analyse

blocks.content: The analyst **watches** users doing their work with the current system and records what happens (e.g. how long tasks take, what problems occur).

blocks.title: Observation
rows: Shows what **really** happens, not what people say happens
People may **behave differently** when they know they are watched
**Reliable, first-hand** information — e.g. times and errors
**Time-consuming**; rare events may not be seen
Finds problems users do not notice or forget to mention
Some people feel uncomfortable being watched
No need to interrupt the work
Does not show users' opinions or reasons

blocks.content: Studying the **paper and electronic documents** of the current system — forms, invoices, receipts, reports, spreadsheets, manuals, logs.

blocks.title: Examining documents
rows: Shows the exact **data items** used — input and output formats for design
Documents may be **out of date**, incomplete or inaccurate
**Quick** and cheap; does not disturb staff
Does **not show opinions** or problems users feel
Shows the **volume** of data (e.g. 300 orders per day)
Can be hard to understand without explanations
Gives facts for the data dictionary and screen layouts

blocks.title: Choosing a method
blocks.content:
- 600 students' opinions about the canteen → **questionnaire** (many people, cheap, anonymous).
- The director's needs for new reports → **interview** (one key person, detail and follow-up).
- How long librarians take to issue a book → **observation** (real times).
- Which data is written on current loan cards → **examining documents** (exact data items).

When a question asks for disadvantages of **two** methods, each answer must be specific to **that** method: "Interview: time-consuming, so **only a few people** can be interviewed" — not a general point that applies to both.

items.title: Quantitative data
items.content: **Numbers**: counts, measurements, ratings, times. Answers "**how many / how much / how often?**". Collected by closed questions, counting and measuring (observation, documents, logs).

items.title: Qualitative data
items.content: **Words**: opinions, descriptions, feelings, reasons. Answers "**why / how do people feel?**". Collected by open questions, interviews and observation notes.

blocks.content: Techniques: **tallying** and frequency tables, **totals**, **percentages**, **mean / median / mode**, **range**, and **charts** (bar, pie, line).

blocks.title: Canteen survey — 200 students answered "How long do you usually wait in the queue?"
blocks.content:
| Waiting time | Students | Percentage |
|---|---|---|
| Under 5 minutes | 36 | 36 ÷ 200 × 100 = **18%** |
| 5–10 minutes | 94 | **47%** |
| Over 10 minutes | 70 | **35%** |
| **Total** | **200** | **100%** |

**Conclusion:** 82% of students wait 5 minutes or more — long queues are a major problem the new system must solve.

pie
  "Under 5 min" : 36
  "5–10 min" : 94
  "Over 10 min" : 70
blocks.caption: Waiting time in the canteen queue (200 students)

blocks.content: **Thematic analysis**: read all the answers, group similar comments into **themes**, count how often each theme appears, and pick **typical quotations**.

blocks.title: Open question "What would you change about the canteen?" — 120 comments
blocks.content:
| Theme | Comments | Typical quote |
|---|---|---|
| Long queues / waiting | 54 | "I spend half the break in the queue." |
| Food sold out | 31 | "My favourite meal is always finished." |
| Paying is slow | 22 | "Cash payment takes ages." |
| Other | 13 | — |

The themes suggest requirements: **pre-ordering**, **showing what is still available**, and **cashless payment**.

blocks.title: Comparing the two kinds of analysis
rows: Objective, quick to analyse, easy to compare and show in charts, large samples
Rich detail; explains **reasons** and motives; finds unexpected problems
No reasons or context — says *what*, not *why*
Subjective, slow to analyse, small samples, hard to compare

blocks.title: Use both
blocks.content: Analysts usually **combine** both: numbers show **how big** a problem is; words explain **why** it happens. Checking one method's results against another is called **triangulation**.

theory.title: Using data collection to develop a new system

blocks.title: From collected data to the new system
items: **Plan** the fact-finding: what to find out, from whom, with which method.
**Collect** the data (questionnaires, interviews, observation, documents).
**Analyse** it — quantitative (counts, percentages) and qualitative (themes).
**Describe the current system**: inputs, processes, outputs, storage (often as a DFD).
List the **problems** of the current system and the **needs** of each user group.
Turn each problem and need into a **requirement** for the new system.
Agree the requirements with the client.

blocks.title: Example — school library: from findings to requirements
rows: Observation: issuing a book takes 3 minutes on paper cards
The system must issue a book by **scanning barcodes** in under 10 seconds
Documents: 15% of loan cards have missing return dates
The system must **record the loan date and due date automatically**
Questionnaire: 64% of students forget return dates
The system must **send a reminder** two days before a book is due
Interview with the librarian: needs a monthly report of popular books
The system must produce a **monthly report** of the most borrowed books

blocks.content: A strong answer always links **method → finding → requirement**. Examiners reward requirements that clearly come **from the scenario**.
There is usually more than one way to solve a problem. The analyst lists the alternatives and compares them against the requirements before recommending one.

items.title: Typical alternatives
items.content:
- Buy **off-the-shelf** software.
- Have **bespoke** software written.
- **Adapt** existing software (e.g. a spreadsheet or database template).
- **Improve the manual** system without computerising it.
- Use a **cloud / online service** (subscription).

items.title: Criteria for comparing
items.content:
- How well it meets the **requirements**.
- **Cost** — buying, development, training, running.
- **Time** to introduce it.
- **Hardware** and compatibility with existing systems.
- **Ease of use** and training needed.
- **Support**, security, reliability, future growth.

blocks.content: Each criterion gets a **weight** (how important it is); each solution gets a **score** (1–5) for every criterion; score × weight are added up. The highest total is the best solution.

**Recommendation:** off-the-shelf booking software scores highest (45). If online booking that matches the centre's needs *exactly* were essential, the weight of "fit to requirements" could be raised — then the bespoke app might win. The weights must come from the client's priorities.

blocks.title: Feasibility (TELOS)
blocks.content: Each alternative is also checked for **T**echnical, **E**conomic, **L**egal, **O**perational and **S**chedule feasibility. An alternative that fails one of them (e.g. too expensive, cannot be ready in time) is rejected.

Alternative solutions can also be **different algorithms** for the same task. They are compared by **correctness**, **time efficiency** (number of steps), **space efficiency** (memory) and **ease of implementation**.

blocks.title: Searching 10 000 book records by ID
blocks.content:
- **Linear search**: works on unsorted data, but up to **10 000** comparisons.
- **Binary search**: data must be **sorted**, but at most **14** comparisons (2¹⁴ = 16 384 ≥ 10 000).
- Since searches happen hundreds of times a day and records are added rarely, keeping the records **sorted and using binary search** is the more effective solution.
The agreed list of **what the new system must do** and **the conditions it must meet**. It guides the design and is used at the end to **evaluate** the system.

items.title: Functional requirements
items.content: What the system must **do** — its functions. "The system must allow teachers to **add and delete** student records." "The system must **email** a weekly report to parents."

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.content: **How well** it must work — performance, security, usability, reliability. "A search must return results in **under 2 seconds**." "Only staff with a password can **edit** marks."

items.title: Hardware and software requirements
items.content: What is needed to run it. "Runs on **Android 10** or later." "The server needs at least **8 GB RAM**."

blocks.title: Good and poor requirements
rows: "The timetable must load in under 3 seconds."
"The system should be easy to use."
"A new user must be able to place an order without training in under 2 minutes."
"Each user must log in with a username and a password of at least 8 characters."
A design decision, not a need
"The system must store records of at least 2000 students."

blocks.title: Writing requirements from a scenario
items: Underline every **task** the users do and every **problem** mentioned.
Write each as "The system **must** …" with **one** function per requirement.
Add **measurable** values where possible (time, number, size).
Include **security** and **usability** needs.
Check that each requirement can be **tested** at the evaluation stage.

blocks.title: Requirements from a scenario (Paper 2 style)
blocks.content:
*A student wants to develop a mobile app for schoolteachers to keep records of classroom achievements and homework, which are currently kept manually. Teachers should be able to add and delete students, assign homework to classes and send records to students and parents.*

1. The app must allow teachers to **add and delete student records**.
2. The app must allow teachers to **assign homework to a class**.
3. The app must **send** records and results to students and parents automatically.
4. The app must let teachers **record achievements** for each lesson.
5. Each teacher must **log in** with a password so that only they can change their classes' records.

blocks.title: Priorities — MoSCoW
blocks.content: Requirements are often labelled **M**ust have, **S**hould have, **C**ould have, **W**on't have (this time), so the most important ones are built first.

blocks.title: Model answers
blocks.content:
**Q: State two disadvantages of using questionnaires and two disadvantages of using interviews when collecting data. [4]**
- Questionnaire 1: low response rate — many people do not return it (1).
- Questionnaire 2: questions cannot be explained, so they may be misunderstood (1).
- Interview 1: time-consuming, so only a few people can be interviewed (1).
- Interview 2: not anonymous, so people may not give honest answers (1).

**Q: State one advantage of analysing existing documentation. [1]**
It shows the exact data items and formats used by the current system (1).

**Q: Explain why an analyst might use both quantitative and qualitative data. [2]**
Quantitative data shows how many people have a problem / how big it is (1), and qualitative data explains why the problem happens / users' reasons (1).

- Writing the same disadvantage for two different methods ("it takes time").
- Calling a closed question "qualitative" — closed answers give **quantitative** data.
- Writing vague requirements ("the system should be good") instead of specific, testable ones.
- Forgetting to link the answer to the **scenario** in the question.
